question.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{1}{x+1}{y}^{′}+({x}^{2}+1)y=0,\,x>0.
$$

Suppose ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are solutions and their Wronskian $W(x)$ satisfies $W(1)=6.$ What is $W(3)?$

$W(3)=$ {{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
Abel's identity says that if ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are solutions of

$$
{y}^{″}+P(x){y}^{′}+Q(x)y=0,
$$

then their Wronskian $W(x)$ satisfies

$$
{W}^{′}(x)=-P(x)W(x).
$$

In our equation, the coefficient of ${y}^{′}$ is 

$$
P(x)=\frac{1}{x+1}.
$$

Substituting into Abel's identity gives

$$
{W}^{′}(x)=-\frac{1}{x+1}W(x).
$$

Now, we solve the first-order differential equation for $W:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{W}^{′} & =-\frac{1}{x+1}W \\ \frac{\text{d}W}{W} & =-\frac{1}{x+1}\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{\text{d}W}{W} & =\int -\frac{1}{x+1}\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|W| & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+K \\ |W| & ={e}^{K}(x+1)^{-1} \\ W & =\frac{C}{x+1}\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a constant.

Next, we use the given value $W(1)=6$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}W(1) & =\frac{C}{1+1} \\ 6 & =\frac{C}{2} \\ C & =12\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
W(x)=\frac{12}{x+1}.
$$

Finally, we compute $W(3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}W(3) & =\frac{12}{3+1}=3.\end{aligned}
$$
